Assignment: Weekly e-Journal Reflection
Objective: The Weekly e-Journal Reflection is designed to foster critical thinking and personal reflection on the content covered in the course, including lectures, workshops, and your group project. This reflective exercise aims to help you:
gain insights into your own learning journey;
apply course concepts to your group project as you progress through the semester;
consider the impact of your learning on real-world scenarios; and
develop an understanding of the broader impact of real-life IT issues on society, organizations, and ethics.
Assignment Structure:
Submission of Weekly Entries:
Create a new entry in your e-journal each week, covering weeks 1 to 10 of the course.
Each entry should be concise, approximately half a page (up to 200 words) and submitted via Canvas.
Each entry should be added to your previous entries. That is, your final e-journal submission be a single document with all weekly reflections from 1-10.
Content of Weekly Entries:
Describe an aspect of the course that you have personally experienced during the week. This could include material covered in lectures (including guest lectures), tutorials, or your group project.

Content of Weekly Entries:
Describe an aspect of the course that you have personally experienced during the week. This could include material covered in lectures (including guest lectures), tutorials, or your group project. It may include tasks such as research, software testing, planning and running meetings with your sponsors and mentors, or any noteworthy experiences related to your project.
Reflect on the experience, detailing any actions you personally took, what you personally have learned, and how you can apply this insight to your project in the coming weeks.
You may consider the following aspects:
Benefit to Society: Discuss the potential impact of your project work on society or a specific community.
Value to Organization: Reflect on how your project tasks contribute to the goals and objectives of the organization or project sponsor.
Ethical Issues: Analyse any ethical dilemmas or challenges encountered during your work, including team conflict and resolution, fairness in workload allocation, or the proper use of resources.
At least one weekly entry should relate to feedback you receive for the Project Proposal and how you plan to apply it.
At least one weekly entry should relate to lecture or tutorial content.
Multimedia Elements:
You have the option to include multimedia elements such as images, videos, or relevant files to enhance your reflection.
Timely Submission:
It is encouraged to submit your weekly reflections at the end of each week, as this will be considered during the marking process.
The final submission should contain a consolidation of all previously submitted weekly reports.

Weekly reflection is due every Sunday by 23:59 from week 1 onwards, till the 10th week. You need to submit it every week in the same drop box. See FAQs – ITS Capstone Units for more on the weekly journal.
Evaluation Criteria: Your weekly e-journal reflections will be assessed based on the following criteria:
Critical Analysis and Relevance: The depth and relevance of thought and analysis in your reflections.
Application of Learning to Improving your Project : Demonstration that your analysis and reflection will contribute to a better outcome for your project through tangible actions. Use of feedback and lecture material as well as group experiences are included in the application of your learning.
Communication and Presentation: The organization, structure and clarity of your writing.
Timeliness: The submission of reflections at the end of each week is encouraged and is included in the assessment.
Submission: Submit your weekly entries with your latest entry at the top.

Starter team roles – Guidance Notes
How to use these role descriptions
These roles are a starting point, not a fixed structure. Every project is different, and your team should adapt the roles to suit your project, sponsor, mentor, team size, and final outputs.
In a small team, one person may hold more than one role, and some roles may be shared. The key point is that your team agrees who is accountable for each responsibility. Accountable means making sure the work is planned, followed up, completed, and recorded - not necessarily doing all the work yourself.
Teams should review their roles regularly, especially if the project changes direction. Pay particular attention to basic project management tasks that are easy to miss, including recording decisions, tracking scope changes, sending minutes, managing issues and risks, and checking progress against the timeline.
A useful test is:
A useful test is: when something needs to be done, does the team know who is responsible for making sure it does not get dropped? If something goes wrong, do we know who was responsible for making sure it was followed up?
A role is useful only if it helps the team communicate, make decisions, and deliver the project more effectively.

You have already been in a bunch of meetings, what did you see?

Strategise:

How does the sponsor meeting fit - what role does it play?

 • Who are the stakeholders - you, your team, your sponsor . Is anyone else
 going to be involved? What are their interests; what's in it for them?
 • How will you tell if the visit has met its aims?

Plan/design:

Work out a sort of meeting script that will cover the topics in a logical order:

 • Determine the materials you'll provide – early thoughts, progress reports in
 further meetings, background of the topics for discussion.
 • Work out what you need to achieve from the meeting – what information
 you want to provide, and what information you require from the
 sponsor/other participants.
 • Plan the logistics - place, time, security and access, parking, presentation

 • Make sure everyone has mobile numbers in case of problems.

Develop/test:

Prepare all the necessary materials and walk through the meeting in situ.

Act :

Contact each participant, send agenda and materials, put meeting into their diaries.

 • Meet and greet on the day - see the hints from your research (above)
 • Stick to the allocated time – don’t be late and don’t run over time.

Follow-up and review:

 • Write up notes of the meeting, decisions and actions allocated to specific

35

 Peer evaluation (individual), 3%

 The 3% mark is given to you for submitting a valid peer evaluation of the other members of your
 team. It is your opportunity to evaluate how well each of them contributed to the team project.
 It is an important component of the group assessment and one of the skills that a project
 manager must learn and apply (reward and consequence) in a real‐world setting.
 Product vs process
 You are FAIRLY assessing /evaluating:
 • the process, rather than the outcome
 • ability to work with diverse team members with different personalities.
 The peer evaluation index (PEI), which is the average percentage score from the peer evaluations,
 will be used to obtain each person’s individual score for the final group assignment.
 Individual score for the final assessment is calculated as follows:
 E = ((E1+E2+E3)/2 x PEI + (E1+E2+E3)/2))
